title: Alaska
description: In California, there are no true education freedom options in which tax dollars follow the student. The only option is publicly controlled charter schools.
body:
# CURRENT GRADE: D

**There are no options for tax dollars to follow the student for private school but there are a variety of publicly funded school options.**

**Homeschooling is very parent friendly and there are publicly funded options such as correspondence schools.**

**Compulsory attendance is required between ages 7-16.**

# Education Options

- [Correspondence Schools](https://education.alaska.gov/compass/ParentPortal/ExploreOptions)
- Program that provides funds to homeschoolers or high school students learning independently.
- Multiple enrollment options and curriculum choices.

- [Charter Schools](https://education.alaska.gov/alaskan_schools/charter)
- Publicly funded.
- No limit on number allowed - currently there are 54.

- [Alternative Schools](https://education.alaska.gov/compass/ParentPortal/ExploreOptions)
- Alternative schools support students who need help finding a different path to academic success that may not be found in a traditional school setting. Alternative schools most commonly support students who are significantly behind in course credit.

- [Residential Schools](https://education.alaska.gov/compass/ParentPortal/ExploreOptions)
- Offer students access to academic and extra-curricular opportunities in a residential setting that are unavailable to students in their home schools and communities.

# Homeschooling Laws

**Here are [state requirements](https://hslda.org/post/how-to-comply-with-alaskas-homeschool-law) on the topic of homeschooling:**

- Variety of options for homeschooling.
- If you are the parent or legal guardian providing the instruction there are no requirements to notify, seek approval, etc.

**Religious Exemptions:**

- There are no state specific religious exemption laws.

The First Amendment states “Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, *or prohibiting the free exercise thereof*.” Many argue that a religious conviction to provide a home-based education is constitutionally protected and a state religious exemption law is not a requirement to be able to homeschool on religious grounds.

It should be noted that the U.S. Supreme Court in [*Wisconsin v. Yoder (1972)*](https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/406/205/#tab-opinion-1949691) established that “Under the Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment, a state law requiring that children attend school past eighth grade violates the parents’ constitutional right to direct the religious upbringing of their children.” (The case involved a challenge of a 16-year-old student to be exempt, so the scope was limited)
